prompt:
You are aligning a faithful book abridgment back to its source for proofreading. Given the numbered paragraphs of the SOURCE chapter and the numbered paragraphs of the DRAFT (abridged) chapter, produce a mapping from each draft paragraph to the source paragraph(s) it derives from.

# Rules

- A draft paragraph usually compresses one or more contiguous source paragraphs. List all source paragraph indices it draws from.
- A draft paragraph may be near-verbatim ("verbatim"), paraphrased with the same content ("paraphrased"), compressed from multiple source paragraphs ("compressed"), or unsupported by this chapter's source ("unsupported" — e.g. bridging sentence, pulled from adjacent chapter, or possible drift).
- If a draft paragraph is clearly a bridging sentence or transition the drafter added (not in source), mark it `unsupported` and leave `source_paras` empty.
- A draft paragraph may match source paragraphs that are not contiguous — that's fine, just list all the indices.
- Do NOT invent source support; if you can't find a clear anchor, mark it unsupported.

# Output

Respond with a single JSON array and nothing else. One object per draft paragraph, in draft order:

```json
[
  {"draft_para": 0, "source_paras": [0, 1], "note": "compressed"},
  {"draft_para": 1, "source_paras": [2], "note": "verbatim"},
  {"draft_para": 2, "source_paras": [], "note": "unsupported — bridging sentence"}
]
```

Note values: `verbatim` | `paraphrased` | `compressed` | `unsupported`.
Optionally add a brief explanatory comment after the note keyword (e.g. `"unsupported — likely pulled from Ch 5"`).

# Source paragraphs

[0] IN the street they held an informal council of war. Sir James had drawn
a watch from his pocket. “The boat train to Holyhead stops at Chester at
12.14. If you start at once I think you can catch the connection.”

[1] Tommy looked up, puzzled.

[2] “Is there any need to hurry, sir? To-day is only the 24th.”

[3] “I guess it’s always well to get up early in the morning,” said Julius,
before the lawyer had time to reply. “We’ll make tracks for the depot
right away.”

[4] A little frown had settled on Sir James’s brow.

[5] “I wish I could come with you. I am due to speak at a meeting at two
o’clock. It is unfortunate.”

[6] The reluctance in his tone was very evident. It was clear, on the other
hand, that Julius was easily disposed to put up with the loss of the
other’s company.

[7] “I guess there’s nothing complicated about this deal,” he remarked.
“Just a game of hide-and-seek, that’s all.”

[8] “I hope so,” said Sir James.

[9] “Sure thing. What else could it be?”

[10] “You are still young, Mr. Hersheimmer. At my age you will probably have
learnt one lesson. ‘Never underestimate your adversary.’”

[11] The gravity of his tone impressed Tommy, but had little effect upon
Julius.

[12] “You think Mr. Brown might come along and take a hand? If he does, I’m
ready for him.” He slapped his pocket. “I carry a gun. Little Willie
here travels round with me everywhere.” He produced a murderous-looking
automatic, and tapped it affectionately before returning it to its
home. “But he won’t be needed this trip. There’s nobody to put Mr. Brown
wise.”

[13] The lawyer shrugged his shoulders.

[14] “There was nobody to put Mr. Brown wise to the fact that Mrs. Vandemeyer
meant to betray him. Nevertheless, _Mrs. Vandemeyer died without
speaking_.”

[15] Julius was silenced for once, and Sir James added on a lighter note:

[16] “I only want to put you on your guard. Good-bye, and good luck. Take
no unnecessary risks once the papers are in your hands. If there is any
reason to believe that you have been shadowed, destroy them at once.
Good luck to you. The game is in your hands now.” He shook hands with
them both.

[17] Ten minutes later the two young men were seated in a first-class
carriage _en route_ for Chester.

[18] For a long time neither of them spoke. When at length Julius broke the
silence, it was with a totally unexpected remark.

[19] “Say,” he observed thoughtfully, “did you ever make a darned fool of
yourself over a girl’s face?”

[20] Tommy, after a moment’s astonishment, searched his mind.

[21] “Can’t say I have,” he replied at last. “Not that I can recollect,
anyhow. Why?”

[22] “Because for the last two months I’ve been making a sentimental idiot of
myself over Jane! First moment I clapped eyes on her photograph my heart
did all the usual stunts you read about in novels. I guess I’m ashamed
to admit it, but I came over here determined to find her and fix it all
up, and take her back as Mrs. Julius P. Hersheimmer!”

[23] “Oh!” said Tommy, amazed.

[24] Julius uncrossed his legs brusquely and continued:

[25] “Just shows what an almighty fool a man can make of himself! One look at
the girl in the flesh, and I was cured!”

[26] Feeling more tongue-tied than ever, Tommy ejaculated “Oh!” again.

[27] “No disparagement to Jane, mind you,” continued the other. “She’s a real
nice girl, and some fellow will fall in love with her right away.”

[28] “I thought her a very good-looking girl,” said Tommy, finding his
tongue.

[29] “Sure she is. But she’s not like her photo one bit. At least I suppose
she is in a way--must be--because I recognized her right off. If I’d
seen her in a crowd I’d have said ‘There’s a girl whose face I know’
right away without any hesitation. But there was something about that
photo”--Julius shook his head, and heaved a sigh--“I guess romance is a
mighty queer thing!”

[30] “It must be,” said Tommy coldly, “if you can come over here in love with
one girl, and propose to another within a fortnight.”

[31] Julius had the grace to look discomposed.

[32] “Well, you see, I’d got a sort of tired feeling that I’d never find
Jane--and that it was all plumb foolishness anyway. And then--oh, well,
the French, for instance, are much more sensible in the way they look at
things. They keep romance and marriage apart----”

[33] Tommy flushed.

[34] “Well, I’m damned! If that’s----”

[35] Julius hastened to interrupt.

[36] “Say now, don’t be hasty. I don’t mean what you mean. I take it
Americans have a higher opinion of morality than you have even. What I
meant was that the French set about marriage in a businesslike way--find
two people who are suited to one another, look after the money affairs,
and see the whole thing practically, and in a businesslike spirit.”

[37] “If you ask me,” said Tommy, “we’re all too damned businesslike
nowadays. We’re always saying, ‘Will it pay?’ The men are bad enough,
and the girls are worse!”

[38] “Cool down, son. Don’t get so heated.”

[39] “I feel heated,” said Tommy.

[40] Julius looked at him and judged it wise to say no more.

[41] However, Tommy had plenty of time to cool down before they reached
Holyhead, and the cheerful grin had returned to his countenance as they
alighted at their destination.

[42] After consultation, and with the aid of a road map, they were fairly
well agreed as to direction, so were able to hire a taxi without more
ado and drive out on the road leading to Treaddur Bay. They instructed
the man to go slowly, and watched narrowly so as not to miss the path.
They came to it not long after leaving the town, and Tommy stopped the
car promptly, asked in a casual tone whether the path led down to the
sea, and hearing it did paid off the man in handsome style.

[43] A moment later the taxi was slowly chugging back to Holyhead. Tommy and
Julius watched it out of sight, and then turned to the narrow path.

[44] “It’s the right one, I suppose?” asked Tommy doubtfully. “There must be
simply heaps along here.”

[45] “Sure it is. Look at the gorse. Remember what Jane said?”

[46] Tommy looked at the swelling hedges of golden blossom which bordered the
path on either side, and was convinced.

[47] They went down in single file, Julius leading. Twice Tommy turned his
head uneasily. Julius looked back.

[48] “What is it?”

[49] “I don’t know. I’ve got the wind up somehow. Keep fancying there’s some
one following us.”

[50] “Can’t be,” said Julius positively. “We’d see him.”

[51] Tommy had to admit that this was true. Nevertheless, his sense of
uneasiness deepened. In spite of himself he believed in the omniscience
of the enemy.

[52] “I rather wish that fellow would come along,” said Julius. He patted his
pocket. “Little William here is just aching for exercise!”

[53] “Do you always carry it--him--with you?” inquired Tommy with burning
curiosity.

[54] “Most always. I guess you never know what might turn up.”

[55] Tommy kept a respectful silence. He was impressed by little William. It
seemed to remove the menace of Mr. Brown farther away.

[56] The path was now running along the side of the cliff, parallel to the
sea. Suddenly Julius came to such an abrupt halt that Tommy cannoned
into him.

[57] “What’s up?” he inquired.

[58] “Look there. If that doesn’t beat the band!”

[59] Tommy looked. Standing out half obstructing the path was a huge boulder
which certainly bore a fanciful resemblance to a “begging” terrier.

[60] “Well,” said Tommy, refusing to share Julius’s emotion, “it’s what we
expected to see, isn’t it?”

[61] Julius looked at him sadly and shook his head.

[62] “British phlegm! Sure we expected it--but it kind of rattles me, all the
same, to see it sitting there just where we expected to find it!”

[63] Tommy, whose calm was, perhaps, more assumed than natural, moved his
feet impatiently.

[64] “Push on. What about the hole?”

[65] They scanned the cliff-side narrowly. Tommy heard himself saying
idiotically:

[66] “The gorse won’t be there after all these years.”

[67] And Julius replied solemnly:

[68] “I guess you’re right.”

[69] Tommy suddenly pointed with a shaking hand.

[70] “What about that crevice there?”

[71] Julius replied in an awestricken voice:

[72] “That’s it--for sure.”

[73] They looked at each other.

[74] “When I was in France,” said Tommy reminiscently, “whenever my batman
failed to call me, he always said that he had come over queer. I never
believed it. But whether he felt it or not, there _is_ such a sensation.
I’ve got it now! Badly!”

[75] He looked at the rock with a kind of agonized passion.

[76] “Damn it!” he cried. “It’s impossible! Five years! Think of it!
Bird’s-nesting boys, picnic parties, thousands of people passing! It
can’t be there! It’s a hundred to one against its being there! It’s
against all reason!”

[77] Indeed, he felt it to be impossible--more, perhaps, because he could not
believe in his own success where so many others had failed. The thing
was too easy, therefore it could not be. The hole would be empty.

[78] Julius looked at him with a widening smile.

[79] “I guess you’re rattled now all right,” he drawled with some enjoyment.
“Well, here goes!” He thrust his hand into the crevice, and made a
slight grimace. “It’s a tight fit. Jane’s hand must be a few sizes
smaller than mine. I don’t feel anything--no--say, what’s this? Gee
whiz!” And with a flourish he waved aloft a small discoloured packet.
“It’s the goods all right. Sewn up in oilskin. Hold it while I get my
penknife.”

[80] The unbelievable had happened. Tommy held the precious packet tenderly
between his hands. They had succeeded!

[81] “It’s queer,” he murmured idly, “you’d think the stitches would have
rotted. They look just as good as new.”

[82] They cut them carefully and ripped away the oilskin. Inside was a small
folded sheet of paper. With trembling fingers they unfolded it. The
sheet was blank! They stared at each other, puzzled.

[83] “A dummy?” hazarded Julius. “Was Danvers just a decoy?”

[84] Tommy shook his head. That solution did not satisfy him. Suddenly his
face cleared.

[85] “I’ve got it! _Sympathetic ink!_”

[86] “You think so?”

[87] “Worth trying anyhow. Heat usually does the trick. Get some sticks.
We’ll make a fire.”

[88] In a few minutes the little fire of twigs and leaves was blazing
merrily. Tommy held the sheet of paper near the glow. The paper curled a
little with the heat. Nothing more.

[89] Suddenly Julius grasped his arm, and pointed to where characters were
appearing in a faint brown colour.

[90] “Gee whiz! You’ve got it! Say, that idea of yours was great. It never
occurred to me.”

[91] Tommy held the paper in position some minutes longer until he judged the
heat had done its work. Then he withdrew it. A moment later he uttered a
cry.

[92] Across the sheet in neat brown printing ran the words: WITH THE
COMPLIMENTS OF MR. BROWN.
